name: Hana Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What fills your working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a string quartet, play violin, record parts for small films and teach two advanced pupils. I have a master's degree in music and twenty-nine years of paid work. I love the moment four players stop counting and start breathing together, though invoices and file permissions eat too much of the afternoon.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does that mean for your household, and how do you use technology now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, my husband repairs bicycles and our grown children live elsewhere. The quartet and recordings pay well, we have fourteen months of expenses saved, and several ensembles work nearby. I use AI every day for rehearsal notes and to flag passages to check, but I listen myself and keep pupils' names and clients' unreleased recordings out of it. I value a family business and a proper paid apprenticeship more than an unpaid promise.

I would say **four quartet players** still need to hear one another.
think: Our **fourteen-month reserve** and workshop income cover an ordinary cancellation.
The **quartet and sessions** should continue through mild AI.
do: Confirm **quartet dates**, session rates and recording permissions in writing.
Use **approved AI notes** only on nameless passages; listen before sharing and exclude client recordings and pupil names.
feel: I feel **calm** about booked work and household income.
S0.quote: A tidy note cannot take the place of four paid chairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the quartet that a faster rehearsal note is fine if the four of us still hear one another and our recording terms stay written. Small AI conveniences would not change the ticket price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fourteen months saved and my husband's workshop income make an ordinary cancelled show manageable. I expect the live quartet, film sessions and two pupils to carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll confirm the spring quartet dates, film-session rates and recording permissions in writing. In the first year of mild AI I'll keep using my approved note tool on nameless passages, listen before sharing any suggestion and keep client recordings and pupil names out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about work already booked. A tidy note cannot take the place of four paid chairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who catches a wrong note?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second violin caught a wrong bowing in a machine note last week. I changed the note before rehearsal rather than telling her the software was right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a client track go into the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a client film track stays in its licensed folder. I use a short tune I own when I need a test file.

I'd request **stated quartet fees** and recording rights.
think: Film sessions supply **one fifth** of my own income and could shrink.

do: Separate **film invoices** from live fees and request written rates and permissions.

feel: I feel **anxious** about a realistic session-fee loss.
S1.quote: A free credit on a film is not a fee for four musicians.
fieldNote: The **film-session fifth** of her income is exposed to cheaper generated cues.

steps.text: Separate film invoices from live fees; request written rates and permissions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our booking agent that generated film cues may undercut paid string sessions. I'd insist a client choose between a licensed track and four musicians at a stated fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Film sessions are about a fifth of my income, and that part could shrink soon. The quartet concerts and pupils still pay, but I would not let an agent call a vague future credit a session fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll separate a year's film invoices from live quartet fees and ask the agent for a written rate and permission for every recording. In the first year I'll try a new AI cue-comparison tool only on my own licensed music, if the ensemble pays my review time and every player consents; I'll check it by ear and stop if it copies a client file or saves no paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about that fifth of my income. The savings let me refuse a free demonstration that spends the other players' rights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the agent paid for the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the agent has not offered review pay or obtained the other players' consent. I can test on a tune I wrote, but not on their unreleased takes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a credit replace pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A free credit on a film is not a fee for four musicians. I would ask for a signed rate before recording.

Seek **booked live work** with net after rehearsal/travel replacing lost fees; use reserve temporarily if absent.

S2.quote: Fourteen months saved is a bridge, not a monthly pension payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the players that thinking AGI by 2028 may replace film cues long before playing robots arrive around 2031. I would put signed live quartet dates and our recorded-music rights in one folder now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the film-session fifth of my income to go quickly. I do not expect every live ticket to go in 2028, though robots three years later could test that assumption.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll get the film and concert amounts in writing, check who owns our original recordings, called masters, and request an actual pension estimate without choosing a retirement date. In the first year after 2028 I'll keep the quartet's paid concerts and two pupils, decline any digital reuse without each player's consent and a signed licence fee, and replace the lost session money only with booked live work that pays after rehearsal and travel costs; if no such booking exists, I'll use savings while seeking one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a fifth disappearing, even with fourteen months saved and ensembles nearby. The first empty film invoice will sting more than a dramatic headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who owns the recorded masters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We own some old quartet masters together, but each new client's agreement is different. I will read the actual rights clause before approving a reuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the reserve mean retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No pension figure has arrived. Fourteen months saved is a bridge, not a monthly pension payment.

Renew only when **paid attendance** covers all playing/rehearsal/travel fees under same safe insured stage/cancellation terms; decline otherwise.
feel: I feel **anxious** about film loss with time to quote a paid season.
S3.quote: A hall's applause will not pay the second violin's fare.
fieldNote: She **prices four musicians**, rehearsal and travel before accepting a hall residency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the quartet that full AGI by 2031 gives us time to renegotiate a live residency before playing robots arrive around 2034. I would ask a hall for a paid season, not a publicity slot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The film work may fade before 2031. A residency could help, but only if its guaranteed fees cover four players, rehearsal and travel rather than shifting the risk to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This season I will ask two halls for written residency terms naming paid dates, each musician’s playing and rehearsal share, travel, recording rights, cancellation pay, and hall-provided safe stage space with venue insurance at no charge to us. In the first year after 2031, if film sessions have gone, I will take a residency only when a signed contract guarantees all four players’ fees and those costs outside existing paid concert and pupil dates; otherwise I will keep already paid concerts and pupils and seek separate booked calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about likely film-fee loss, but five years lets us quote as a group. A hall's applause will not pay the second violin's fare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has a hall offered a fee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One hall has invited us to talk, not offered a fee. I would send a price for the whole quartet before reserving a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a second season viable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would renew only after counting paid attendance against all four players’ playing and rehearsal fees and travel, with the same safe insured hall-provided stage and written cancellation terms. If that floor failed, we would finish contracted shows and decline the next season.

Our **fourteen-month reserve** and workshop income cannot prove pension sufficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grown children that full AGI by 2036 gives me ten years to read pension figures and choose which paid seasons to play. Playing robots follow around 2039; no calendar date tells me what the pension office will pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might still want the quartet. Fourteen months saved and my husband's workshop income help, but neither tells us whether stopping work pays our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll request actual pension statements, price two more seasons of quartet dates and set aside half of each extra cleared film-licence fee after bills and musicians' shares toward eighteen months saved. In the first year after 2036 I'll keep only paid concerts and pupils that cover my playing, rehearsal and travel; I'll agree to a new recorded reuse only with every player's consent and signed licence pay, and decide whether to reduce work only after comparing a pension confirmed payable for that period and paid fees with household costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about paid seasons that far away, while our current reserve and work are strong. I would choose fewer quartet concerts from payable pension and paid-fee figures, not from my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if licensing pays nothing extra?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If licensing produces no extra fee, there is no half to move into savings. The other players' shares and our bills come first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would read the pension figures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband and I would read the actual pension statement together. I will not turn down a signed quartet date on the strength of a guessed payment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the film sessions could end before our live calendar is firm. Signed quartet dates, a clear rights clause, paid replacement calls and the actual pension statement would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the other three players what a generated recording does to their fees. I can lead the quartet, but I cannot sign away the other three players’ music to protect my own chair.

portrait: Hana is a **58-year-old senior violinist** with a music master's, husband and grown children.
Her **higher pay**, fourteen-month reserve and nearby ensembles give room to respond to threatened film fees.
She **uses AI daily** on nameless notes but guards player consent and client recordings.
She seeks a **fully paid quartet residency** and bases later work choices on actual pension figures.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase Hana's film-session fifth before the live quartet calendar is secure.
